explanations.answer: So they know they have eternal life
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, friend. The writer says, "I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you may know that you have eternal life." (1 John 5:13) He doesn't want his readers guessing or crossing their fingers. He wants them to KNOW.

explanations.answer: So they can answer false teachers
explanations.explanation: Good guess, baker, but that's not the reason he gives here. The writer says he wrote "…so that you may know that you have eternal life." (1 John 5:13) Nothing in this verse mentions false teachers. He keeps his eyes on what believers can know.

explanations.answer: So they will write back to him soon
explanations.explanation: That's not in this verse, friend. The writer says he wrote "…so that you may know that you have eternal life." (1 John 5:13) His goal is what his readers know. Nothing here is about a reply.
That's the way, baker. "If we ask anything according to His will, He hears us." (1 John 5:14) Notice he says anything, and he says He hears. The key is asking in line with what God wants.

I can see why you'd pick that one, friend, but fasting and tears aren't what this verse names. It says, "If we ask anything according to His will, He hears us." (1 John 5:14) The way he points to is asking according to His will.

Nope, no compass needed, baker! Nothing in this verse is about which way you face. It says, "If we ask anything according to His will, He hears us." (1 John 5:14) The way is according to His will, and you can ask from the kitchen floor.

Careful, friend, it's the other way around. The writer says, "And if we know that He hears us in whatever we ask, we know that we already possess what we have asked of Him." (1 John 5:15) He doesn't leave believers unsure. He says we know.

That's right, baker. The text says, "And if we know that He hears us in whatever we ask, we know that we already possess what we have asked of Him." (1 John 5:15) So believers can be sure, not stuck wondering. Lots of us check the oven ten times, but here the writer says we know.

Yes, baker. The writer says he "…should ask God, who will give life to those who commit this kind of sin." (1 John 5:16) So he asks God for his brother, and God is the One who gives life. Asking is the action the verse names.

That's a reasonable thought, but it's not what this verse says. The writer says the believer "…should ask God, who will give life to those who commit this kind of sin." (1 John 5:16) The action here is asking God. Elders aren't mentioned in this passage.

I get the instinct, friend, but this verse doesn't say that. The writer says the believer "…should ask God, who will give life to those who commit this kind of sin." (1 John 5:16) The action it gives is asking God for his brother.

Close, baker, but the writer says the opposite. He says, "There is a sin that leads to death; I am not saying he should ask regarding that sin." (1 John 5:16) He does tell believers to ask about the other kind of sin. For this one, he says he is not saying to ask.

That's right, friend. The writer says, "There is a sin that leads to death; I am not saying he should ask regarding that sin." (1 John 5:16) He tells believers to ask for the sin not leading to death, and he doesn't say to ask about this one. The text doesn't tell us more than that.

Yes, baker, protects is the word. "the One who was born of God protects him, and the evil one cannot touch him." (1 John 5:18) Anyone born of God has someone watching over him. That's a better deal than my old junk drawer, where the only protection was a rubber band.

I see why that word came to mind, friend, but it's not the one here. The writer says, "the One who was born of God protects him…" (1 John 5:18) Nothing in this verse is about a test. It's about being kept safe.

Easy to reach for that one, baker, but the verse says something warmer. "the One who was born of God protects him, and the evil one cannot touch him." (1 John 5:18) The word is protects. Anyone born of God has that protection.

That's right, friend. The writer says, "the One who was born of God protects him, and the evil one cannot touch him." (1 John 5:18) The protection and the "cannot touch" come together. Read it twice, it's good.

Not this time, baker, because that statement is true. The writer says "the One who was born of God protects him, and the evil one cannot touch him." (1 John 5:18) Notice who does the protecting: the One who was born of God, not the person himself. That's a lot of weight to put on a single verse, and it holds.

explanations.answer: The power of the evil one
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The writer says, "…the whole world is under the power of the evil one." (1 John 5:19) He sets that next to "…we are of God…" Two very different places to stand.
Good thinking, baker, but the writer never mentions Caesar here. He says, "…the whole world is under the power of the evil one." (1 John 5:19) That's the power the verse names.
Nice try, friend, but this verse says nothing about Moses' law. The writer says, "…the whole world is under the power of the evil one." (1 John 5:19) That's the power it names.

Yes, baker. The writer says the Son of God "…has given us understanding, so that we may know Him who is true…" (1 John 5:20) Understanding is what He gave, and it leads to knowing Him. That's a gift better than any fresh batch.

I can see why you'd think that, friend, but authority isn't the gift named here. The Son of God "…has given us understanding, so that we may know Him who is true…" (1 John 5:20) The gift is understanding, and its aim is knowing Him, not being in charge of anything. Then the verse says "…we are in Him who is true…" So knowing Him and being in Him sit side by side.

Commandments are all over the Bible, baker, but not in this spot. The writer says the Son of God "…has given us understanding, so that we may know Him who is true…" (1 John 5:20) The word is understanding, and it's given so we may know Him.
Whoa, friend, the writer says the opposite. He says, "…we are in Him who is true—in His Son Jesus Christ." (1 John 5:20) Believers aren't far away. They're in Him.
You got it, baker. The writer says, "…we are in Him who is true—in His Son Jesus Christ." (1 John 5:20) Not far away, but in Him. That's about as close as it gets.

That's right, baker. The last line of the letter says, "Little children, keep yourselves from idols." (1 John 5:21) After all that talk about the true God, he ends with a warning to stay away from idols. Short and strong.
Good thought, friend, but riches aren't named here. This closing line says, "Little children, keep yourselves from idols." (1 John 5:21) The word is idols.

I see why you'd pick that, baker, but strong drink isn't named in this verse. Right before it, the writer says of Jesus Christ, "He is the true God and eternal life." (1 John 5:20) Then comes the closing line, "Little children, keep yourselves from idols." (1 John 5:21) I think those two lines sit together on purpose. Once the letter has pointed to the true God, an idol is something set up in His place, so the last word is to keep away from those.
